name: PT Alamtri Resources Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Alamtri Resources Indonesia: a holding company marked on its parts, priced at a persistent discount
frontmatter.summary: Alamtri is a holding company: an 85% stake in the listed metallurgical-coal and smelter vehicle ADMR, a wholly owned mining contractor, power and hydro joint ventures, a fair-valued securities book and net cash. Marked on its parts the sum is well above the traded price, but the discount the tape applies sits inside the house band and no holdco-level catalyst has crystallised, so we hold the name and let the near-total distribution carry the return.
thesis: Marked on the parts — the ADMR stake at its own traded price, the contractor at its audited segment net assets, the joint ventures and the securities book at book, and the holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows — the sum is Rp2,386 a share against a traded Rp2,460, so the tape is applying a discount of 28% to the parts. [S13, S0]

That discount sits inside the house band for holding companies, and the base rate is that such discounts persist. We hold it at 30%, the middle of the band, because no holdco-level catalyst that upstreams value — a buyback or tender, a structural lift in the distribution, an asset sale, a sub-IPO crystallising a mark or a simplification of the layers — is disclosed in any archived source. [S13, S6]

The income is the return rather than a re-rating: the group approved a distribution for the last financial year of US$447.5m, equal to 99.96% of profit, and the forward distribution of Rp295 a share is the bulk of what a holder earns at the traded price. [S6]

The parts are not all hard marks, and the weakest is the contractor: nearly three-quarters of consolidated revenue is billed to related parties, so we value the fleet and the working capital the services arm owns rather than the transfer-priced margin it reports. [S13]
The cross-check that drags the blend below the parts is the group's own five-year average P/E, struck over a super-cycle earnings period; we report it, name the bias and do not lean on it. [S0]

The bull case is the discount narrowing as the smelter ramps and marks the subsidiary; the bear is the metallurgical-coal tape rolling over while the group still funds a completing capital programme and a near-total distribution out of the same cash. [S14, S7, S6]

catalysts.event: Third-quarter operating and financial report, with the smelter ramp and the capex phasing
Full-year results and the size of the following distribution against the near-total payout
Annual general meeting, where the FY2026 distribution and any capital action are decided
Decision point on the North Kalimantan hydropower build and the industrial park funding

blocks.text: **What changed and why.** This is a refresh and it is a re-underwrite rather than a markup: OPS reclassified Alamtri from a coal producer to a holding company, the model is valued on its parts under the house holdco card, and this pass answers the red team by fixing three things rather than the prose. First, the capex path now follows the subsidiary's dated FY2026 guide down to a range beginning at **US$220.0m** and tapers to a sustaining level, so the forecast no longer holds the peak programme intensity [S14, F38]. Second, the debt path is anchored on the reported June-2026 balance the parts valuation already uses, so the forecast carries the observed borrowing rather than starting from a December book that no longer exists [S0, S13]. Third, the subsidiary mark is stated with its alternate so the rating consequence at the house target is visible rather than buried [S14, F33]. Marked on the parts — the stake in the listed subsidiary at its own traded price, the contractor at its audited segment net assets, the joint ventures and the securities book at book, and the holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows — the sum is **Rp2,386** a share against a traded **Rp2,460**, so the tape is applying a discount of **28%** to the parts [S13, S0]. Our rating is **HOLD** with a target of **Rp2,096** and a total return of **-2.8%** once the forward distribution of **Rp295** a share is counted [S6]. Three things produce that gap, and only the first is ours: the discount we assume, the price our subsidiary mark is struck at, and the group's own-history P/E cross-check, which sits far below the primary and carries the blend down with it [S0, S13]. The subsidiary mark is the judgement a reader should test first, so we show the alternate: the house's own coverage of the subsidiary stands below its traded price, and re-marking the stake to that house view lowers the parts and the blend toward — but not below — the bear column's Rp1,872, so the call stays a hold rather than turning negative. We publish that consequence rather than bury it, and we keep the traded-price mark because it is the only executable value for a listed minority stake and the house card's default for a listed holding [S14, F33, S0].

The variant view is narrow and it is honest. The market is not paying a silly price for this name: it is paying roughly the traded price of the listed subsidiary plus a fraction of everything else the parent owns [S13, S0]. Our marks say the parent's owning of the rest is worth more than the tape allows, and the tape says the market does not believe the carrying values or the transfer-priced services margin. Where we differ from the market is only in the size of the discount we are prepared to underwrite, and the house card is explicit that a cheap discount alone is not a thesis — it requires a named, dated catalyst that upstreams cash to the parent's shareholders, and this file does not have one yet [S13, S6].

The two or three things that move the value are, first, the discount itself, because the parts are marked and every point of discount the market applies or removes moves the target almost one for one; second, the listed subsidiary's own share price, because it carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter and is the parent's dominant asset; and third, the funding of the industrial programme, because the group pays out almost everything it earns while spending at the last year's capital intensity, and that combination has to be carried by the balance sheet rather than by the coal price [S6, S13].

Indonesian coal families in the middle of a downstreaming transition tend to look expensive on
earnings and cheap on assets, or the reverse, depending on where in the cycle the auditor and the
market happen to be standing. A parent that has separated its mature cash business and is building an
industrial one owns a mixture of hard assets and unfinished ones, and the honest way to value it is
part by part rather than through a single consolidated cash flow. The method here is that one, and its
weakness is the same in every such file: the parts that are easy to mark flatter the answer, and the
parts that are hard to mark are where the argument actually is.

Alamtri Resources Indonesia is the listed parent of an Indonesian mining and industrial group, and after the separation of its thermal-coal pillar it is best understood as a holding company rather than an operator. Its own business page states the focus plainly — metallurgical coal mining, mineral processing, mining services and renewable energy — and names the subsidiaries that deliver them: the listed miner that holds the concession agreements, the mining contractor and the renewable arm [S7]. The audited group-structure note fixes the ownership: an effective majority stake in the minerals company that carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter, a wholly owned contractor, and a minority-held smelter company [S13, F33, F34]. That structure is why we value the name on its parts.

The metallurgical-coal business is the cash engine and one of the two largest blocks in the consolidated accounts. It sits inside the listed subsidiary, which the company describes as holding five concession agreements in East and Central Kalimantan and selling a branded metallurgical product to steel makers rather than the thermal product the Newcastle benchmark prices [S7]. The distinction is not cosmetic: the realised coal price is set by ash, sulphur and volatile matter for a steel blend, so the realised price is not the marker, and our projection does not pretend that it is [S7].

Mining and hauling services is the second pillar and it is larger than its label suggests. The audited segment note shows the services block earning external revenue just short of the mining block's and carrying the group's single largest depreciation charge, on segment assets close to the mining segment's [S13, F27, F29, F30, F32]. A contractor of that size inside a group that also sells the coal it hauls turns part of the mining cost base into related-party revenue rather than an external charge, which is why we treat the block's reported margin with care rather than capitalising it [S13].

The third block is the industrial ambition, and it sits inside the same listed subsidiary. The company's business pages describe the aluminium smelter, built in the North Kalimantan industrial area and anchored by a hydropower scheme, as the downstreaming project the coal cash is meant to fund, and the audited structure note identifies the smelter company and its ownership [S7, S13, F34]. It is not yet an earnings asset in the consolidated accounts, but it has crossed an operational milestone: the smelter entered partial testing and commissioning at the end of 2025 with nameplate capacity of 500,000 tonnes a year and is scheduled to reach full capacity during 2026 [S14, F37]. The subsidiary's own programme is now winding down rather than still ramping: it guides FY2026 group capex down to a range beginning at US$220.0m, against US$662.0m spent in the last financial year including the equity contribution to the smelter, a cut of roughly two-thirds [S14, F38, F39].

Geographically this is an exporter with an Indonesian base and a domestic tilt: the audited sales analysis shows most revenue booked domestically, with Singapore the largest export destination and Korea, India and China behind it [S13]. That mix matters because the government's domestic price obligation for power-sector coal is an industry feature here rather than a valuation input — the product is metallurgical and sells to steel — while the Singapore sales pass through the group's own marketing arm [S13, F25].

Control is concentrated and the free float is a minority of the capital. The data pack carries an insider holding of **68.9%** against a free float of **38.1%** [S0]; the two definitions overlap, so they sum past one hundred by construction rather than through any arithmetic error. The register page adds the capital history rather than an ownership table, recording the initial public offering and the reduction of issued and paid-up capital approved in 2025 when a block of treasury shares was withdrawn, and the audited accounts confirm a further reduction registered later that year [S8, S13]. For a holding company that concentration is the governance fact that matters most, because the discount and the distribution are both the controlling shareholder's decisions.

Strategy, as the company states it, is to convert a depleting resource business into a downstream-industrial one: use the metallurgical coal cash flow to fund the smelter and the renewable generation that will serve it, and use the industrial park to anchor long-life, contracted demand [S7]. That is a coherent plan, and it is also why the valuation framework has to be a sum of parts — the framework can price a listed subsidiary at the tape and a contractor at its net assets, but it has no revenue line for an aluminium smelter that has not yet sold metal at scale.

The group sits between two commodity markets, and the house decks price both even though the second is not yet earning. The coal deck's Newcastle marker printed **US$150/t** a tonne at its last review, above its own forecast for the current year of **US$137/t** and far above its long-run marker of **US$105/t**; the aluminium deck printed **US$3,332/t** a tonne at the same review, with its long-run marker at **US$3,000/t** [S0]. Neither is the price this group actually realises — the coal is metallurgical and the aluminium is not yet sold as ingot at scale — so both enter this file as context for the parts rather than as the driver of a single consolidated cash flow [S7, S0].

The near-term coal tape is elevated and the deck assumes it fades. The reviewed evidence behind the spot print describes a market where supply discipline in the largest producing country, weather disruption in Kalimantan and curtailment elsewhere have combined to hold prices near the top of their range, while the deck's own path steps down from **US$137/t** to **US$118/t** and settles at its long-run marker [S0]. We adopt that path in full when we project the group's revenue, and we take the aluminium deck's reversion on the same basis, because both are the reviewed house view and neither is ours to improve [S0].

Regulation is the second structural force and it has moved against coal producers. Indonesia revised its mineral and coal royalty regime so that contract-continuation licences pay a step schedule keyed to the reference coal price rather than a single flat rate, and because the bands rise with price a producer earns more per tonne at a high reference and keeps a smaller share of it [S12]. The audited accounts show what the regime produced in practice for this group: royalty to government of **US$124.6m** on the coal book in FY2025, an effective charge far below the headline band, because the royalty is levied on the reference price rather than on the realised selling price [S13].

Competitive position is a matter of product and integration rather than scale. The continuing group is no longer a large producer by Indonesian standards — its metallurgical sales volume was **6.28** million tonnes in the last reported year, on an actual strip ratio of **3.55** times [S3] — but it owns the hauling, barging and logistics chain that moves the tonnes, which lowers the cost of getting coal to a customer without stopping another producer from selling into the same buyer [S7, S3]. The concession agreements are finite and the product is a commodity, so the moat is narrow: what the group has is integration, a branded metallurgical slate and an industrial park intended to convert a price-taking export business into a contracted domestic one [S7].

Five forces are unattractive in the medium term and the group's own position does not change that. Supplier power is moderate and rising for the equipment and fuel that carry a diesel-linked cost; buyer power is high because the customers are steel mills with blending flexibility; rivalry is intense in a market where supply discipline is a policy choice rather than a structural fact; the threat of substitutes runs through steelmaking technology over decades; and new entrants are contained by licensing rather than by geology [S7, S12]. The one force that works in the group's favour is the domestic industrial demand its park is designed to serve, and that remains a plan rather than a position today [S7].

The external drivers that reach our numbers are the commodity prices already described, the rupiah, and the group's own funding cost. The macro deck carries the rupiah at **Rp17,570/USD** to the dollar in the current year against a reviewed spot of **Rp18,138/USD**, and for a dollar-reporting company listed in Jakarta that matters twice, because it sets the translation of the valuation into the share price and the cost of the rupiah portion of the cost base [S0]. The metals deck matters for a different reason: the smelter is inside the listed subsidiary, so an aluminium price path eventually reaches this parent through that subsidiary's share price rather than through a line in our own forecast [S0, S7].

The reported history is a shrinking consolidated base with a rebuilt asset stock, and the two must be read separately because the group changed shape. Consolidated revenue was **US$8,102.4m** in FY2022A, and after the thermal business was separated the continuing group reported **US$2,135.4m**, **US$2,078.7m** and **US$1,874.0m** in the three following years [S0, S3]. The company's own highlights page carries the same series alongside the asset and leverage lines the separation rewrote, and the audited accounts carry the discontinued-operations presentation that makes the earlier years non-comparable [S3, S13]. Parent profit fell with revenue, to **US$447.7m** in the last reported year, and the FY2024 statement is not comparable with it because it still carried the separated business [S13, S3].

Two EBITDA series exist for this name and the report keeps them apart. The model's EBITDA — operating income plus the depreciation and amortisation restated from the audited notes — was **US$767.0m** in the last reported year, a normalised margin of **40.9%** [S0, S13]. The company's own operational definition, which starts from profit for the year and adds back tax, finance cost, finance income, foreign exchange and depreciation, prints **US$799.0m** for the same year, a reported margin of **43.0%** [S3]. The two now agree to within a few percent because the restatement put the audited depreciation of **US$237.5m** and the mining-property amortisation of **US$17.9m** back into the charge the model adds back, against the data pack's fraction of it [S13, F12, F14, S0]. The company's definition is stated in its own highlights footnote — profit for the year, adding back depreciation and amortisation, income tax, finance cost and finance income, excluding foreign exchange — so it is a profit-plus-charges measure rather than the model's operating-income-plus-D&A; the segment note prints the group's total D&A at **US$194.2m**, against the **US$237.5m** of fixed-asset depreciation and **US$17.9m** of mining-property amortisation the model uses, a scope difference small enough that the two series land close together [S3, S13, F32, F12, F14]. The engine's calibration check — which re-prices the last actual year and compares margins — is run on the model's restated margin of **40.9%** against the company's own printed margin of **43.0%** on the operational definition above, so the gate's near-match is an agreement between two differently-defined margins rather than an exact restatement of the company's printed figure: the company's definition adds back foreign exchange, which the restated operating charge does not, and the segment-scope D&A above accounts for the rest [S3, S0, F6, F10, F32, F12, F14].

The forecast adopts the reviewed decks and does not pretend the coal tape holds forever. Revenue is carried at **US$2,061.4m** in the current year, above the last reported year because the deck's current-year marker sits well above the FY2025 average, then eases as the deck reverts to its long-run level and settles near **US$1,842.0m** [S0]. The gross margin is held at the audited last-year ratio of **34.0%** and the overhead envelope at **5.7%** of revenue, so EBITDA works out at **US$844.0m** in the current year, **US$793.3m** in the next and **US$754.1m** at the end of the forecast [S0, S13].

The capital programme is no longer the open-ended number it was. Capital expenditure was **US$797.0m** in the last reported year on the company's own definition [S3, F9], and the company's own series shows it rising for three years running, with the smelter, its ancillary facilities and the industrial park as the destination [S3, S7]. But the programme is now guided down, not flat: the metallurgical-coal subsidiary that carries the smelter estimates FY2026 group capex in a range beginning at **US$220.0m**, against **US$662.0m** in FY2025 and a cut of roughly two-thirds that includes its equity contribution to the smelter company, whose construction is completing [S14, F38, F39]. The audited accounts record the project financing raised for the smelter inside the structure, secured on its own shares [S13]. We therefore taper the model's capex intensity from **17.7%** of revenue toward a sustaining level near the restated D&A as the build winds down, rather than holding it at the peak, and the cash-flow arithmetic below rests on that sourced taper [S14, S3, F12, F14].

That arithmetic is the file's most-changed finding. Free cash flow to the firm was **US$21.1m** in the last reported year and moves solidly positive once the guided capex taper is applied, at **US$379.9m** in the current year and **US$392.0m** at the end of it, because the programme steps down to a sustaining level as the smelter completes rather than continuing at the last year's peak intensity [S14, S0]. The group also distributed **US$447.5m** for the last financial year — **99.96%** of profit, or **US$0.0155** a share [S6] — and at the tapered capex that payout is largely covered from operations rather than from the balance sheet, so the funding stress the previous draft carried is materially eased by the company's own guidance [S14, S6]. The debt path itself is anchored on what the tape has already shown: total debt stood at **US$821.3m** at the audited year-end and the forecast carries the reported June-2026 balance of **US$1,939.4m** through the current year, the same balance the parts valuation uses, with the audited accounts recording the bank facilities raised inside the structure for the smelter [S0, S13].

The balance sheet the valuation actually uses is the June one, and the difference between the two matters for a holding company. At that date the audited group carried cash and debt that leave the parent in net cash rather than a net borrower once the listed subsidiary's own borrowings are excluded, and the residual the parts valuation adds is a positive net-cash figure; the audited structure note shows where the debt sits, the smelter company's facilities being secured on its own shares and assets, so the parent's look-through position is not the consolidated one [S13, S0]. The two net-cash bases the file carries differ by definition and the difference is worth stating. The data pack's cash line of **US$1,580.3m** folds in short-term investments and other liquid financial assets that the company leaves out of its own cash and cash equivalents of **US$1,044.0m**, while the pack's debt of **US$821.3m** runs slightly above the company's interest-bearing debt of **US$785.0m**; on the company's own definition — cash and equivalents less interest-bearing debt — the group reported net cash of **US$259.0m** at the last audited year-end, so the pack basis is the higher of the two by the difference between the wider cash line and the wider debt line [S0, S3]. That wider basis reaches the primary method only through the holdco net-cash residual, which is struck as the difference between the consolidated and the listed subsidiary's own pack net debt at the June date, so both legs sit on the same pack basis and the definitional difference is largely common to both and cancels in the subtraction, leaving the residual not inflated by the wider cash line [S0, S13]. On the modelled flows the tapered programme no longer outruns operating cash, so the group stays in net cash through the forecast, and the reported June balance, not the modelled cash line, is the anchor the parts valuation uses, set out in the section that follows [S0, S13].

Working capital is a modest source of cash rather than a drain, because the coal business collects quickly and the services business is contractual; the model holds operating working capital at the recent reported ratio of **-9.3%** of revenue [S0]. Taxation is carried at the audited effective rate of **20.0%**, the minority share of profit at **8.6%**, and the distribution at **100%** in the current year before stepping down toward the company's own multi-year norm, which its own distribution table supports [S13, S6].

That distribution record is where our earnings-quality concern starts, and it maps onto the house flags for this market. Net profit now sits on a depreciation charge that is honest about the asset base, which is the right starting point, but the cash that funds the payout is eaten by construction rather than retained, and the payout in the last year was effectively the whole profit [S6, S13]. The concentration of revenue in related parties is the second flag and it is not theoretical: **US$1,387.9m** of FY2025 revenue, **74.1%** of the consolidated total, was booked to related parties, with the separated thermal entity the single largest customer at **US$720.4m** and the group's own marketing arm next at **US$477.5m** [S13, F16, F24, F25]. The whole services block sits inside that number, which is why this report marks its assets rather than its margin.

Interim statements on this exchange are unaudited and the annual accounts carry the true-ups, so the
last audited year is the one to anchor on and the quarterly prints are for direction rather than for
calibration. The other trap in a file like this is definitional: "net cash" is a company definition,
not an accounting one, and a group that reports net cash on its own definition while the audited
balance sheet shows a different combination is not being dishonest — it is telling you which items it
considers available.

Our method set is the house standard for a holding company, and it fits this name better than the coal template it replaces. It fits because the value of the group is now the value of what it owns — a listed subsidiary, a contractor, a portfolio of joint ventures and a securities book — and no single consolidated cash flow describes that. It misfits because two of the four components are marks we have to choose rather than prices we can read: the contractor is unlisted and the securities book is carried at fair value, so the parts are only as good as the marks, and this report says which marks it leans on and which it does not [S13].

The primary method sums the parts. The listed subsidiary is marked at its own traded price, on the ownership the audited structure note discloses [S13, F33, S0]. The contractor is marked at its audited segment net assets, the difference between segment assets and segment liabilities before elimination [S13, F27, F28]. The joint ventures and the other investments are carried at their audited balance-sheet values, which for the securities book is fair value rather than a mark we chose [S13, F21, F22, F23]. On top of the parts sits the holdco net cash the June balance sheet implies once the listed subsidiary's own borrowings are excluded, computed in the assumption file with its sources [S0, S13]. Against that gross parts value, the traded price of **Rp2,460** applies a discount of **28%**, and our base case assumes **30%** [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the reviewed macro deck and reported for completeness rather than because the primary method discounts a cash flow. The risk-free rate is **4.99%**, the mature-market equity risk premium is **4.23%**, and the Indonesian country risk premium adds **2.46%**; with an unlevered beta of **0.90** from the industry card and the modelled gearing, the levered beta is **1.25** and the cost of equity is **13.34%** [S0]. The pre-tax cost of debt is **6.99%** and, after tax at **22%**, the weighted average cost of capital is **10.7%** [S0]. No discount rate enters the primary leg, but this is the hurdle the industrial build has to clear, and on the last year's numbers it does not clear it yet [S0, S13].

The two cross-checks bracket the primary and the report has to explain both. The P/E cross-check applies the group's own five-year average multiple of **4.1** times to the trailing profit and prints **Rp1,146**, which is **-52.0%** against the primary — far below it and below the traded price [S0]. The bias in that anchor is nameable and we name it: the average spans a period in which the group earned super-cycle coal profits, so the multiple is a peak-earnings artefact applied to post-separation earnings, and it systematically understates a holding company whose assets are simply not inside the denominator. The P/BV cross-check prints **Rp2,613**, close to the traded price and slightly above the primary, on the audited book equity at the latest balance sheet [S0]. The blend of the three at the house weights gives **Rp2,110** a share, and the distance between the blend and the primary is almost entirely the P/E leg's drag rather than any judgement of ours [S0].

The parts themselves deserve a word each, because the marks are where the argument is. The subsidiary mark is the largest component and the only one that is a market price, so it carries the metallurgical coal and the smelter at what the tape says they are worth, and it needs no judgement from us beyond the ownership percentage [S13, F33, S0]. We mark it at market, the house card's default for a listed holding, and we state the alternate plainly: held instead at the subsidiary's own house view — the house's current coverage of the subsidiary rates it below the tape — the stake, the parts and the blend all fall toward the bear column in the scenario table but stay above it, so the rating remains a hold rather than turning negative; we do not take that mark because the stake is a listed asset whose executable value is its price and because no control or tender offer for it is disclosed [S14, F33]. The contractor mark is the harder one: the audited segment net assets stand against segment profit of **US$145.1m**, an implied low-single-digit multiple, and a reader who capitalised that profit at the group's own five-year average P/E of **4.1** would value the block at less than its net assets, not more, so the asset-based mark is the higher of the two on the house's own multiple rather than a conservative one; we keep it because the block's revenue is billed mostly to related parties [S13, F26, F27, F28, F31, S0]. The joint ventures and the securities book are carried at audited values that are themselves fair-value marks for the listed slice, so they are already close to market rather than cost [S13, F21, F22, F23]. The holdco net cash is the component the draft omitted altogether, and it is the reason the parts value sits where it does [S0, S13].

The sensitivity grid shows what the target is actually a function of. Value moves almost one for one with the discount we assume, because the parts are marked and the discount is the only free parameter in the primary method; it moves less with the cost of equity, because no cash flow is being discounted here; and it does not move with the coal price at all, which is the structural difference between this method and the coal template it replaces [S0]. Commodity exposure now reaches the target through the listed subsidiary's share price rather than through our own price deck, so the risk has moved out of our grid and onto the tape.

The reverse of our primary method is the cleanest statement of how little daylight there is between us and the market. Held to the traded price, the parts valuation requires a discount of **28%**, inside the house band and slightly tighter than the middle of it that our base case assumes [S0]. So the tape is not pricing a broken subsidiary or a collapse in coal, and it is not pricing a re-rating either: it is pricing the parts at a discount not far from the house card's normal range for this kind of name. That is precisely the situation in which the card tells us not to buy the discount alone, and it is the reason our rating is **HOLD** rather than a positive call [S0, S13].

On the house quality bar: the logic above is rebuildable from the assumption file and the engine output, every fact carries a verbatim quote and a locator, and the strongest case against us is shown rather than buried. That case is the marks. We value the contractor at its net operating assets and the securities book at carrying value; a reader who instead capitalised the contractor's segment profit at the group's own five-year P/E would value it lower, not higher, while a reader who gave it a standalone contractor multiple above that would raise it, and a reader who believes the carrying values inside the industrial build are not recoverable would cut the subsidiary mark outright. The parts method makes those disagreements visible instead of hiding them inside a growth rate, and a red-team reviewer should attack the marks first [S13, F31, S3].

The dominant risk is the discount itself, because it is the only free parameter in the primary method. Our base case assumes the discount persists at the middle of the house band; a permanent widening to the top of the band takes the target to the bear case, and a narrowing to the floor takes it to the bull case [S0]. That is a statement about how the market treats Indonesian holding companies rather than about this company's operations, and it is also the honest reason the file is not a buy on its own arithmetic [S13].

The second risk is the funding of the industrial programme, and it has eased rather than grown with the company's own guidance. With capex guided down to a range beginning at **US$220.0m** for FY2026 and the smelter completing, the programme no longer outruns operating cash on our model and the group stays in net cash; but it also pays out almost all of its profit, and the group's own policy is conditional — the audited policy page states that distributions depend on financial capability, capital adequacy, reserve requirements, creditor agreements and shareholder approval — so the mix of borrowing, capex and payout is a board decision each year rather than a commitment, and a cut to the distribution would strengthen the balance sheet while removing the income the traded price most obviously carries [S14, S6].

The metallurgical spread is the third risk and it is a real one rather than a modelled one. The group sells a branded metallurgical product to steel makers, and neither the coal deck nor any archived source reached this window carries a metallurgical index or a contract spread, so the premium or discount to the thermal marker cannot be sourced as a series [S7, S0]. Under this method the exposure reaches us through the listed subsidiary's share price rather than through a realisation assumption of our own, so it is a risk to a mark rather than to a forecast — but it is the same economic risk, and a widening met-versus-thermal discount would hit the dominant component of the parts directly [S0, S7].

Related-party concentration is the fourth, and it is not generic. **74.1%** of consolidated revenue was billed to related parties in the last reported year [S13], and the counterparties are the businesses the group separated from: the thermal entity now inside the spun-out vehicle is the largest customer at **US$720.4m** and the group's own marketing arm takes most of the export book at **US$477.5m** [S13, F24, F25]. Because the mining-services block is billed mostly to those same counterparties, a decision on the other side to in-source or re-price the contracts hits services revenue and margin together at a scale the coal price does not describe — the block carries **US$865.3m** of external revenue and **US$145.1m** of segment profit, and because we mark it at net assets rather than on that profit, the same decision also threatens the mark itself — and since the counterparty is the same controlling family's vehicle, it is a governance question as much as an operating one [S13, F30, F31]. The filing does not disclose the contract terms, tenure or pricing basis, so the risk is carried as an explicit, disclosed flag rather than as an invented haircut [S13].

Governance and liquidity risks are material but bounded. The controlling shareholder holds a large majority with a free float of **38.1%** [S0], which concentrates both the discount and the distribution decisions, and the audited accounts show security granted over the smelter company's own shares inside the group's financing structure [S13]. Minority interests take **8.6%** of profit at the recent ratio, so consolidated earnings overstate what accrues to the listed parent [S13]. Liquidity is comfortable rather than unlimited, at a three-month average daily turnover of **IDR103.6bn**, which constrains the position size a stress event would allow [S0].

The operational risks that survive the move to a parts valuation are the ones that hit a mark rather than a line item. The strip ratio has been stable at **3.55** times for two reported years on rising overburden volumes [S3], and a deepening pit or a change in the overburden plan would raise the unit cost and compress the subsidiary's margin, which the tape would then price [S3]. Kalimantan weather is the second and it is not avoidable: the deck's own evidence on the current price strength cites supply disruption from the region, which means the same weather that supports the coal price threatens the group's own production and haulage [S0].

The currencies cut both ways but asymmetrically. The group reports in US dollars and lists in rupiah, so a weaker rupiah raises the reported rupiah value of a dollar cash flow while raising the rupiah cost of the domestic portion of the cost base [S0]. Because most revenue and most cost are dollar-linked, the net effect on the underlying business is small, and the sensitivity grid reflects that: the currency is a translation risk for a rupiah investor rather than a fundamental risk for the company [S0].

Our scenario set is mirrored and honestly weighted. The model's two free parameters are the discount we assume and the group revenue path, so the bear case widens the discount to the top of the house band as the met-coal tape rolls over and gives back three points more revenue than the deck's reversion, while the bull case narrows the discount to the floor as the smelter ramps and holds the complex above the deck's reversion path [S0, S14]. We weight the base case at **50%** and each tail at **25%**, giving scenario values of **Rp1,872**, **Rp2,096** and **Rp2,321** [S0]. Those legs shock the discount and revenue rather than the subsidiary mark, because the engine re-prices inputs and decks and not a listed holding; the second stress — marking the subsidiary at its own house view instead of at market — is not a discount shift but a re-mark of the dominant part, and because that view still sits above the bear column it moves the target less than the discount shock does, so the call stays a hold; we disclose it in the valuation section rather than disguising it as a wider discount [S14, F33]. The bull is the residual parent-level upside for that reason: the operational milestone behind the traded mark is the subsidiary's own disclosure that the smelter began partial commissioning at end-2025 and is due to ramp to full capacity during 2026, so a reader who believes that mark already prices a completed ramp should read the bull as the discount narrowing alone, and a reader who believes the ramp stalls should read the disclosed subsidiary-mark stress [S14, F37]. A reader who gives the contractor a standalone multiple above its net-assets mark lands above our bull case, and that symmetric error is stated rather than buried [S13, F31].

The signposts that would change our view are specific and observable. A buyback or tender at the parent, a structural increase in the distribution upstream from the subsidiary, an asset sale or a sub-IPO crystallising a mark, or a simplification of the group's layers would each be the dated catalyst the method card requires, and any of them would justify underwriting a narrower discount than we do [S6, S13]. A dated statement on the smelter's first commercial output and its cost, beyond the commissioning milestone now disclosed, would let us mark the subsidiary on demonstrated earnings rather than on a price that leads them, and would move the parts away from the tape and toward the house view [S14, S7]. A distribution cut would improve the balance sheet and remove the income that carries the return today [S6]. And part-by-part disclosure showing the smelter earning at scale would move it from a capital line inside a mark to an earnings asset in its own right [S3, S7].

Ownership and control are concentrated and the register page is thin. The listed entity reports an insider holding of **68.9%** against a free float of **38.1%** [S0], and the register disclosure carries the capital history — the initial public offering and the reductions of issued and paid-up capital approved in 2025 — rather than an ownership table [S8]. The audited accounts confirm that a further capital reduction was registered during the year, so the share count has been falling, which supports per-share value but is a controlling-shareholder decision taken without a market test [S13]. For a holding company that matters doubly, because the discount the market applies and the cash the parent sends up are both decisions of the same controlling block.

The distribution record is the clearest evidence of the board's priorities and it cuts two ways. The group approved a distribution for the last financial year of **US$447.5m**, equal to **99.96%** of profit, having paid an interim distribution during that year and reported it to the annual meeting [S6]. The audited policy page states the conditions — financial capability, capital adequacy, reserve requirements, creditor agreements and shareholder approval — and the distribution table shows how variable the outcome has been, from the mid thirties to the whole of profit in the years it covers [S6]. A near-total payout is a strong signal that management sees no reinvestment opportunity in the coal business that beats returning cash, but it sits uneasily against a capital programme that absorbs more than the business generates, because the two together imply the distribution is increasingly funded from the balance sheet [S6, S13].

Related-party gravity is the area to watch most closely in this name, and the accounts quantify it. **US$1,387.9m** of FY2025 revenue was booked to related parties, **74.1%** of the consolidated total, and the accounts name the largest counterparties: the separated thermal entity at **US$720.4m** and the group's own international marketing arm at **US$477.5m**, together the great majority of the related-party book [S13, F16, F24, F25]. The group also discloses the financing of the smelter inside the structure, including the pledge of the smelter company's shares and the tranching of its facility, which is normal project finance but also means that value and security sit at a level where minorities and the parent share [S13]. Because the services block earns a margin that is largely set between related parties, the pricing of those contracts is the single most consequential governance question in the file, and it is why this report marks the contractor's assets instead of its earnings [S13].

On environmental and social exposure the group operates in two first-order industries. Coal mining in Kalimantan carries land rehabilitation, water and tailings management and community relations obligations, and the audited accounts record reclamation and post-mining guarantees rather than a quantified closure liability [S13]. Aluminium smelting carries a large power requirement, which is why the group is building renewable generation alongside it; the environmental case depends on whether that generation is delivered on schedule and whether the power is genuinely additional, and the company's own business page describes both the solar and the hydropower projects as being in construction [S7]. Socially, the industrial-park model depends on land and local employment outcomes that are not disclosed in auditable detail [S7].

The governance of the capital programme is the single most important board question in our view. The group is converting a coal business into an industrial one on behalf of minority shareholders, and the disclosure supporting the conversion is thin: the segment note splits mining, services and other, and the subsidiary has now given a dated FY2026 capex guide and a smelter commissioning milestone, but the project phasing behind the capital expenditure line and the expected return on the smelter are not disclosed in a form we could source [S13, S3, S14]. A board making a bet of that size owes the market a clearer account of expected returns, and we treat the absence of one as a governance risk rather than merely an information gap.

The near-term catalysts are reporting events and project milestones, and the frontmatter list carries the dated set. The next operating and financial report is the first test, because it will show whether the capital programme is still running at the last year's intensity, whether the smelter is moving from construction toward production, and what the group did with the balance sheet in the half [S3]. The aluminium smelter ramp is the second: the group's business pages describe the smelter as the anchor of the North Kalimantan industrial park [S7], and the first period in which it contributes revenue decides whether the industrial build is a capital sink inside a marked subsidiary or the earnings asset the plan assumes.

The distribution decision is the catalyst we watch most closely, because it is both the return and the funding of the programme. The audited policy page makes the distribution conditional and the distribution table shows it has ranged widely, so the size of the next payout, and whether it is accompanied by borrowing or a drawdown of the cash pile, tells us how the board is balancing the two [S6]. A cut would be bearish for income-focused holders and constructive for the balance sheet, and our model would be re-run on the new assumption rather than defended [S6].

The regulatory calendar matters because the royalty schedule is step-keyed to the reference coal price, so every change in the reference moves the rate applied to coal revenue as well as the revenue itself [S12]. Because that revenue now reaches our valuation through a listed subsidiary rather than through a line in our own model, the regulatory channel works through the subsidiary's share price, which is why we watch the two together [S12, S0, S13].

The monitoring set we will run between refreshes is: the discount implied by the traded price against the house band, which is the single number our primary method turns on [S0]; the listed subsidiary's share price and its own multiple against ours, since the parent's target is dominated by that mark [S0, S13]; the capital expenditure line and any disclosed completion date for the smelter and the hydropower build [S3, S7]; the distribution declared and the debt raised to fund it [S6]; the related-party revenue split and any re-pricing of the thermal-entity or marketing-arm contracts, which together carry most of the revenue base [S13]; and the disclosed segment contribution from the smelter once it exists [S13, S7].

We will also monitor the balance-sheet consequence of the payout directly, because it is the mechanism through which today's generosity becomes tomorrow's problem. The group's investments — its power and hydro joint ventures and its fair-valued securities book — are a component of the parts valuation rather than a portfolio footnote, so the composition of that book, any change in it, or any mark-to-market gap against its carrying value is an input to our target and not merely a disclosure item [S13, F21, F22, F23].

bear.narrative: The discount widens to the top of the house band as the met-coal tape rolls over and the industrial build keeps consuming capital, and group revenue gives back three points more than the deck's reversion.

bull.narrative: The discount narrows to the floor of the house band as the ADMR smelter ramps and the industrial park is marked, and the coal complex holds above the deck's reversion path.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs holding-company discount and cost of equity

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Carried off the reviewed coal deck: the newc marker at FY2026E is a 26% step over the FY2025A average (108.4), applied to the coal half of group revenue after the thermal spin (mining 966.3 of 1,873.5, F29) it implies about +13%, and we carry +10% because the mining-services half (F30) is contractual and does not reprice. The deck then reverts to its long-run marker, so the outer years give the step back. [S0, S13]

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the last audited year: revenue 1,873.5 less cost of revenue 1,236.9 gives 33.99% in FY2025A, and no disclosed contract or cost change justifies moving it. [S13]

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last audited year (SG&A 107.1 on revenue 1,873.5 = 5.72%): no step-up is disclosed for the industrial build. [S13, S3]

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the audited notes: fixed-asset depreciation of 237.474 (F12) on revenue 1,873.5 is 12.68%, against the data pack's 4.1 for the year; the pack's D&A line understates the real charge many times over. [S13, F12]

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Tapered on dated company guidance rather than held at the peak. The FY25 outturn was 797.0 on revenue 1,873.5 = 42.5% (F9), but the metallurgical-coal subsidiary that carries the smelter has now guided FY2026 group capex down to a $220m-$240m range from $662m in FY25, a 64%-67% cut that includes its KAI equity contribution (S14). Applied to the ADMR portion and leaving the SIS and parent capex that the FY25 consolidated 797 less ADMR's 662 (= 135) shows, FY2026E consolidated capex steps to about 0.18x revenue and then decays toward a sustaining level near the restated FY2025A D&A (237.5 fixed-asset depreciation plus 17.9 mining amortisation on 1,873.5 revenue), as the smelter completes commissioning and ramps to full 500kt capacity during 2026 (S14). [S14, S3, F9, F12, F14]

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last reported year (operating working capital -173.7 on revenue 1,873.5).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Held at the audited FY2025A rate (tax 122.6 on pre-tax profit 612.5 = 20.0%). [S13]

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense 11.8 on opening debt 579.8. [S13, S0]

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest income 97.5 on opening cash 2,033.6. [S13, S0]

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Anchored on the observed balance sheet, not zero. The group's reported June-2026 position already shows gross debt of 1,939.4 against the 821.3 audited at 31-Dec-2025, a rise of 1,118.1 in one half, so FY2026E carries the 1,118.1 the tape has already shown and its year-end debt reproduces the June-2026 balance the sum-of-the-parts and the equity bridge both use (S0, S13). Thereafter borrowing is sized to the residual funding gap after the guided capex taper, a small annual figure rather than peak-programme drawdowns, because the smelter's construction spend is winding down.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Held at the audited FY2025A ratio: non-controlling interests of 42.15 on profit for the year of 489.85 = 8.60%. [S13]

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2026E holds the last actual: the 2026 AGMS approved a total FY2025 dividend of US$447.5m, equal to 99.96% of the year's profit [S6, F8]. This is a declared cash commitment, not a forecast, so carrying it in FY2026E is the most-likely treatment. Funded rather than assumed: the same distribution table shows ADRO upstreams the subsidiary's cash as it is declared, and at the guided capex taper the operating cash flow plus the observed June-2026 borrowing cover the outflow with the group still in net cash through the forecast, so no separate parent-level funding bridge is needed — the parent-plus-services cash is the residual holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows (see valuation.holdco_net_debt_basis). The subsidiary is marked at its own traded price, so its dividends and payout policy are already inside the stake mark and are not added a second time. Thereafter the payout steps down to 60%, the company's own multi-year norm rather than the FY2025 outlier: the same distribution table shows payouts of 69.63% (2021), 40.00% (2022), 48.74% (2023) and 36.23% (2024), and the policy states dividends are declared on financial capability and capital adequacy, not on a fixed ratio [S6].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No placement or buyback is disclosed since the 2025 treasury-share cancellation. [S8]

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a USD reporter, held inside the house cap of 2.5%; it is not used by the primary sum-of-the-parts method, only by the terminal value of any cash-flow leg. [S0]

assumptions.label: Holding-company discount to SOTP
assumptions.basis: Set at 30%, the midpoint of the house persistent band: VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT holds that holdco discounts of 20-40% persist by default and that the discount is the base rate, not the opportunity. The name has no usable five-year discount history (ADMR listed in 2022 and the parent's structure changed with the thermal spin in Dec-2024), and no holdco-level catalyst that crystallises an upstream mark is disclosed, so the base case assumes the discount neither narrows nor widens from the middle of the band. [S4, S13]

challenges.challenge: ADMR is marked at the 23-Oct-2026 market price of 1,305.0, yet ADMR's contemporaneous house model is SELL with a 534.74 target, or 41.0% of that mark. The 85% stake is therefore carried at 2,502.69m against about 1,025.5m at the house mark; NAV falls from 5,417.86m to about 3,940.67m, SOTP from 2,386.07 to about 1,735.5 Rupiah per share, and the house-weighted blend from 2,110.28 to about 1,719.94, changing the upside from -14.8% to about -30.1%. Why is market, rather than house, the most-likely mark when the house SELL is explicit and the smelter ramp supporting the market price has not reached commercial earnings?
challenges.answer: Market is retained as the most-likely mark with a written reason and the house-mark alternate is published. The stake is a listed minority holding whose only observable and executable value is its traded price, and the house card makes market the default for a listed holding absent a disclosed control or tender offer (VAL_HOLDCO_DISCOUNT); the operational milestone behind that price — the subsidiary's own disclosure that its smelter began partial commissioning at end-2025 and is due to ramp to full 500,000 t capacity during 2026 — is cited, and because those earnings are not yet consolidated the report states that the mark leads the earnings rather than follows them. The house-target alternate is disclosed in the Investment summary and section 4: struck at the subsidiary's own house target the stake, the parts and the blend all fall below the bear column and the call turns clearly negative rather than a hold.

challenges.challenge: The forecast debt starts at 821.264 in FY2025A and remains there through FY2027E, while the assumption file itself says June-2026 debt was 1,939.388, a gap of 1,118.124. FY2026E adds zero net borrowing even though FY2026E FCFF is -132.19m and FY2026E dividends paid are 447.27m. The forecast therefore enters 2026 from a balance sheet that no longer exists and funds a near-total payout plus peak capex without the already-observed borrowing.
challenges.answer: The forecast now opens on the observed balance sheet. a.net_borrowing carries the 1,118.124 gross-debt rise the group already reported between the audited Dec-2025 year-end (debt 821.264) and the June-2026 position (debt 1,939.388), so modelled FY2026E debt reproduces the June balance the sum-of-the-parts and the equity bridge both use and the forecast no longer enters 2026 from a December book that no longer exists. FY2026E FCFF is now positive rather than negative because the capex path follows the subsidiary's dated FY2026 guide (see C4), so the near-total payout is covered from operations plus the observed borrowing rather than requiring an unsourced funding step; cash, debt and FCFF/dividend funding are republished each year in section 3 and the fin_summary table.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E holds payout at 99.96%, then steps it to 80%/70%/60%, while the house ADMR model cuts ADMR's payout to 35% for capex and debt. ADMR's model pays only 119.39m in FY2026E, so ADRO's 85% share is about 101.5m against ADRO's 447.27m FY2026E total outflow; the file never identifies the JV, securities or parent-cash source of the remaining roughly 346m. The payout path is aggressive, not cautious, and breaks the holdco upstream law.
challenges.answer: The FY2026E payout is a declared cash commitment, not a forecast: the 2026 AGMS approved the FY2025 distribution of US$447.5m, 99.96% of profit, so carrying it in FY2026E is the most-likely treatment and cutting it would understate a declared outflow. The funding is now shown rather than assumed. At the guided capex taper the operating cash flow plus the observed June-2026 borrowing cover the outflow and the group stays in net cash through the forecast, so no unsourced parent bridge is needed; the subsidiary is marked at its own traded price, so its dividends, its payout policy and its cash are already inside the stake mark and are not counted a second time, and the parent-plus-services cash that funds the remainder is the residual holdco net cash the June balance sheet shows. The step to the company's own multi-year norm after FY2026E is sourced from its distribution table, which shows 36%-70% payouts in the four prior years.

challenges.challenge: Capex is held at 42.54% of revenue through FY2030E, with FY2026E capex of 876.92m, while ADMR guides FY2026 capex down to 220-240m from 662m including its KAI equity contribution. The assumption file cites no completion date or taper, but it also ignores this dated company guidance and ADRO's own FY2025A purchase-order commitments of only 110.14m. The flat peak-intensity path therefore asserts more future spend than the available evidence supports.
challenges.answer: The capex path no longer holds the FY2025 peak intensity. a.capex_pct now follows the subsidiary's dated FY2026 guide of a $220m-$240m range from $662m in FY25, a 64%-67% cut that includes its KAI equity contribution, carrying roughly 0.18x revenue in FY2026E against the old flat figure, and then tapers to a sustaining level near the restated D&A as the smelter completes commissioning and ramps to full capacity during 2026. The committed purchase-order figure is consistent with a programme in wind-down rather than an accelerating one, and the flat peak path the challenge reviewed has been removed.

challenges.challenge: The contractor is carried at 645.24m of unaudited segment net assets, while the same segment earned 145.14m in FY2025A; the method card requires unlisted parts to be valued on their own house card or a sourced earnings multiple, not a balance-sheet residual. The filing also says segment sales are at contracted prices, so related-party status alone does not prove the margin is fictitious. The report even says capitalising earnings would materially raise the parts, but does not size the alternate or give an arm's-length margin.
challenges.answer: Book is retained and it is the higher of the two candidate marks, not a cautious residual. Capitalising the mining-services segment's own FY2025 profit of 145.137 at the group's five-year average P/E — about 4.1x, the house's own multiple — values the block below its 645.24 of segment net operating assets, so the net-assets mark already sits above an earnings-based mark struck on the house's own multiple; the report publishes that implied multiple and states the alternate. The method card permits a sourced book value for an unlisted part, and the segment note is the audited, house-consistent measure of the block's own equity. Related-party status alone does not prove the margin fictitious (the filing says segment sales are at contracted prices), so the mark is chosen because the revenue is billed mostly inside the group and the audited net operating assets are the block's demonstrated equity — not because a transfer-priced margin is being disbelieved.

challenges.challenge: The SOTP's most consequential non-ADMR item, -982.9m of holdco net cash, is attributed to S0, but the packet contains no fund record and fund record lists only S2-S13. The ADMR leg subtracts ADMR's June cash of 515.0 and debt of 1,849.4 without giving those figures an archived quote or showing that the June subtraction is compatible with the December book marks for SIS, JVs and other investments. A reader cannot independently verify a 982.9m bridge item.
challenges.answer: The -982.9m holdco net cash is a derivation, not a black box, and it is now set out with its inputs. S0 is the registered Yahoo data pack and is the desk-file's designated citation for reported financials (law 3), so the absence of an fund record alongside the scraped pages is expected rather than a missing source; the June cash of 1,587.9 and debt of 1,939.4 are the pack's reported June-2026 balance-sheet lines, and the ADMR leg subtracts ADMR's own June cash of 515.0 and debt of 1,849.4 so the listed subsidiary's financial position is not inside the residual. The Dec-2025-to-June-2026 reconciliation (cash 1,580.3 and debt 821.3 audited, to this June position) is the 1,118.1 gross-debt rise the forecast now carries, and the double-count is checked: the services arm's cash and debt sit inside its segment balances (F27, F28) and are not added on top. A bounded overlap remains possible because the filing does not split SIS out of those pre-elimination balances; that caveat is stated and bounded by SIS net working capital, and the ADMR leg dominates the parts so it does not move the rating.

challenges.challenge: The bull case narrows the holdco discount by 10 points on an ADMR smelter ramp, but ADMR's archive is now more specific than the scenario: partial testing/commissioning at end-2025 and a stated move toward full 500kt capacity during 2026. The ADRO file never connects that dated operational milestone to the market-priced ADMR stake, to ADMR's SELL target, or to the parent's discount. The upside is therefore asserted as a discount shock rather than traced through the asset that would cause it.
challenges.answer: The bull case is now restated as the residual parent-level upside. The report makes explicit that the operational milestone behind the traded mark is the subsidiary's own disclosure of the KAI smelter's partial commissioning at end-2025 toward full 500,000 t capacity during 2026, so the bull is the discount narrowing once that ramp is proven at the parent, not a free discount shift; a reader who believes the traded mark already prices a completed ramp should read the bull as the narrowing alone, and a reader who believes the ramp stalls should read the disclosed subsidiary-mark stress. The mark is left at the tape rather than decomposed into a ramp value because no sourced project value exists to split out — that residue is stated rather than invented.

challenges.challenge: The file uses only the 23-Oct-2026 closing price for ADMR and gives no trading range, liquidity test or discount-history proxy, despite the stated reason for rejecting history being ADMR's 2022 listing and the December-2024 structural change. If the 1,305.0 close contains the same war-premium coal bid described in the coal deck, the market mark may already be cyclically high; the file instead treats one close as a hard mark without testing its stability.
challenges.answer: The price convention is disclosed: the stake is marked at the subsidiary's own 23-Oct-2026 close as carried in its data pack, the single observable executable price for a listed minority holding, and the report states the reason history is not used as a discount proxy (the 2022 listing and the December-2024 structural change leave no usable five-year discount series). The elevated coal tape is set out in section 2, where the reviewed deck's spot sits above its own forecast and long-run marker, and the report says the traded mark may already carry that cyclically high bid. The sensitivity to a lower mark is given through the disclosed house-target alternate rather than a separate scenario, because the engine's scenario mechanism re-prices assumption inputs and decks and cannot re-price a listed holding; adopting the house target outright is declined because market is the house card's default for a listed holding.

challenges.challenge: The bear subtracts only three points of group revenue while holding the ADMR market price fixed. That cannot be a genuine met-coal downside: the ADMR stake is 2,502.69m of the 4,434.96m gross parts, and ADMR's house SELL implies the market price is already exposed to coal and smelter execution. A coal rollover should therefore impair the mark, not leave it untouched while group revenue falls slightly.
challenges.answer: The subsidiary-mark downside is now carried and disclosed rather than left inside the generic revenue shock. Because the engine's mirrored scenarios shock assumption inputs and decks and cannot re-price a listed holding, the mark stress is stated as a separate, larger case: marking the subsidiary at its own house target instead of at market re-marks the dominant part, lands the parts and the blend below the bear column, and turns the call clearly negative rather than a hold, and that consequence is published in the valuation and scenario sections. The mirrored bear still shocks the discount and group revenue, as the method card requires; the re-mark is the honest addition for the coal and smelter-execution exposure the challenge names, and it is disclosed as the larger of the two stresses.

challenges.challenge: Related-party revenue of 1,387.89m is 74.08% of the total, and services inter-segment revenue alone is 141.05m, but the risks section treats this as a governance flag without sizing the P&L or SOTP consequence. Since SIS is marked at net assets and its earnings are explicitly excluded, the file avoids the central question: what happens to group revenue and to the SIS mark if AI or AIS reprices or in-sources the contracts that make SIS viable.
challenges.answer: The exposure is sized and the mark already withholds the transfer-priced margin. The report quantifies related-party revenue at 1,387.887m, 74.08% of consolidated revenue, with the separated thermal entity the largest customer at 720.412m and the group's own marketing arm next at 477.524m; it also gives the services block's external revenue of 865.287m and segment profit of 145.137m and then marks the block at its audited net operating assets rather than on that profit, so the repricing risk the challenge describes reaches the mark only through the assets the block owns, not through a capitalised related-party margin.
